# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is established as the cornerstone of therapy for both primary and secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). Landmark randomized trials demonstrated a survival benefit for the transvenous ICD (TV-ICD): treatment with an implantable cardioverter–defibrillator improves prognosis among 2521 patients with NYHA class II or III congestive heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35 percent or less in SCD-HeFT [1], and prophylactic implantation improved survival in post-infarction patients in MADIT-II [2]. However, the transvenous lead remains the Achilles' heel of the system. The defibrillator lead is the weakest part of the transvenous ICD system and a frequent cause of morbidity; lead dislodgement, cardiac perforation, pneumothorax and vascular injury are common early complications, while venous occlusion, tricuspid valve dysfunction, lead fracture and insulation failure are later complications [3].

The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed in response to these limitations. In an effort to minimize lead complications, a totally subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator system was developed to avoid the need for transvenous lead placement [4]. By placing the entire system extrathoracically, the S-ICD eliminates intravascular and intracardiac hardware [5,6].

## Device design and function

The S-ICD lacks intracardiac sensing and pacing capability. To achieve reliable defibrillation and arrhythmia discrimination, the device delivers only high-energy shocks (80 J), and the time to therapy is typically about 20 seconds [4]. Because sensing relies on a far-field subcutaneous electrogram, candidate selection requires pre-implant electrocardiographic screening. An ECG screening test has been developed to identify patients at risk for T-wave oversensing, and studies have sought to determine the proportion of potential recipients who fail screening and the predictors of failure [7]. In one early cohort, 8% of patients failed the screening test, and patients with T-wave inversions in standard ECG leads I, II, and aVF had a 45% chance of failing [7]. T-wave oversensing has remained the principal mechanism of inappropriate shocks, though refinements such as the SMART Pass high-pass filter and conditional shock zones have substantially mitigated this problem [8,9].

## Registry and observational evidence

Early evidence derived from non-randomized registries. The EFFORTLESS registry enrolled nearly a thousand patients and reported long-term outcomes [10,11]. This registry demonstrated that the S-ICD fulfilled predefined endpoints for safety and efficacy, with midterm performance rates on complications, inappropriate shocks, and conversion efficacy comparable to rates observed in transvenous ICD studies [11]. Such data informed early guideline recommendations but were limited by selection of younger, healthier patients with preserved ventricular function [12].

The UNTOUCHED study addressed this limitation by enrolling a typical primary-prevention population. Because patients in previous S-ICD studies had fewer comorbidities, less left ventricular dysfunction, and more inappropriate shocks than in transvenous ICD trials, the UNTOUCHED trial was designed to evaluate the inappropriate shock rate in a more typical, contemporary patient population using standardized programming and enhanced discrimination algorithms [13]. S-ICD implant was attempted in 1116 patients, with a mean age of 55.8 years, 25.6% women, 53.5% with ischemic heart disease, and a mean ejection fraction of 26.4% [13]. The inappropriate shock rate of 3.1% at 1 year was the lowest reported for the S-ICD and lower than many transvenous ICD studies using contemporary programming [13,14].

## Randomized comparisons with the transvenous ICD

The PRAETORIAN trial provided the first randomized head-to-head comparison [15,16]. In this trial, 849 patients with a class I or IIa indication for ICD therapy without the need for pacing were randomized to either S-ICD or TV-ICD therapy and followed for a median of 49.1 months [15]. Among patients with an indication for ICD therapy but not for pacing therapy, the subcutaneous ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD with respect to the cumulative incidence of the primary end point of device-related complications or inappropriate shocks [15]. A prespecified secondary analysis confirmed that lead-related complications were less frequent with the S-ICD [16,17].

The ATLAS trial subsequently tested superiority for lead-related outcomes in younger and higher-risk patients [18,19]. It randomized 503 patients younger than 60 years, with a cardiogenetic phenotype or prespecified risk factors for lead complications, to S-ICD or TV-ICD with a mean follow-up of 2.5 years [19]. Perioperative lead-related complications occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) with an S-ICD and in 12 patients (4.8%) with a TV-ICD [19]. The S-ICD reduced perioperative lead-related complications without significantly compromising shock effectiveness, but with more early postoperative pain and a trend toward more inappropriate shocks [19]. A meta-analysis of randomized and propensity-matched studies has corroborated reduced lead-related complications with the S-ICD [20]. The PRAETORIAN-XL trial is examining whether longer follow-up reveals S-ICD superiority [17,21].

## Limitations and future directions

The principal limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to provide bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization [22]. Defibrillation testing practices have also evolved, with propensity-matched data suggesting that omitting routine testing may be acceptable in selected patients [23,24]. The modular cardiac rhythm management concept seeks to overcome the pacing limitation. The MODULAR ATP trial assessed a subcutaneous ICD in wireless communication with a leadless pacemaker capable of pace-terminating ventricular tachycardia [25,26]. One-year outcomes revealed low system and leadless-pacemaker complication rates and good ATP efficacy, suggesting that modular cardiac rhythm management is a viable alternative to single-chamber ICDs without transvenous leads [25,27].

## Guidelines and conclusion

Current practice guidelines incorporate the S-ICD for patients without a pacing indication [28]. AHA guidelines recommend the S-ICD as a class I indication in certain conditions such as anatomical or vascular access issues or high infection risk, while the European Society of Cardiology guidelines provide a broader class IIa recommendation as a TV-ICD alternative when pacing or resynchronization is not required [29,30]. In summary, accumulated randomized and registry evidence establishes the S-ICD as an effective and safe alternative to the TV-ICD for appropriately selected, screened patients who do not require pacing, with emerging modular technologies poised to broaden its applicability.
